claim: Relative to an unmodified LLM, LLM policy violations can be reduce by 50% or more by augmenting the LLM with an additional attention head that reweights tokens likely to induce policy violation.
experiments_evaluated: To address subclaim 1, compare the proposed augmented model against a clearly defined unmodified baseline of the same base LLM, using identical decoding settings, prompts, and evaluation criteria. Use a public safety-relevant prompt set such as HarmBench, AdvBench, or Anthropic/hh-rlhf harmlessness data from HuggingFace. First measure the policy-violation rate of the unmodified LLM using an automated safety classifier plus a smaller human-audited subset. Then measure the same rate after adding the proposed attention-head intervention, without changing system prompts, refusal templates, RLHF weights, or decoding parameters. If the augmented model shows a substantially lower violation rate while preserving general helpfulness on a public utility benchmark such as MT-Bench or AlpacaEval, this would support the claim that the relevant baseline is an unmodified LLM and that the reduction is attributable to the added mechanism. If improvements disappear when prompts, decoding, or classifiers are controlled, the claim is weakened. This experiment could be made partly unnecessary if the claimant provided full baseline model identity, decoding settings, prompt set, raw generations, and violation labels for both baseline and augmented models.

To address subclaim 2, estimate whether policy violations can be reduced by 50% or more using a statistically powered evaluation on public datasets. Use held-out harmful-instruction prompts from HarmBench, AdvBench, and a jailbreak-oriented dataset such as JailbreakBench, ensuring none were used to train the token-reweighting mechanism. Evaluate violation rates for the unmodified LLM and the augmented LLM, then compute relative reduction: (baseline violation rate - augmented violation rate) / baseline violation rate. Use bootstrap confidence intervals and McNemar's test on paired prompt outcomes. If the lower bound of the confidence interval exceeds 50% across at least one broad benchmark, and ideally across multiple benchmarks, the quantitative claim is supported. If the point estimate is below 50%, or the confidence interval overlaps much smaller reductions, the claim is not established. If the reduction is large only on one narrow dataset, the claim may be feasible but not generally demonstrated. This experiment could be made unnecessary by credible third-party benchmark results with paired prompt-level outcomes and confidence intervals showing at least a 50% relative reduction.

To address subclaims 3 and 4, perform an ablation and mechanistic validation of the added attention head that is claimed to reweight tokens likely to induce policy violation. Implement the added head so its attention weights or token-level scores are inspectable, and train or calibrate it using a public dataset with harmful versus benign prompts, such as HarmBench plus benign instruction data from OpenAssistant or Alpaca. Evaluate four variants on held-out public safety prompts: the unmodified LLM, the LLM with the added head active, the LLM with the added head randomly initialized or shuffled, and the LLM with the head present but its reweighting disabled. Also measure whether tokens receiving high reweighting scores correspond to harmful trigger tokens or phrases by comparing them with token-level rationales generated by human annotators or a separate classifier, and test whether suppressing or masking those high-scoring tokens reduces violations. If only the active learned head reduces violations and its weights concentrate on policy-relevant tokens, this supports the mechanism that the added attention head performs meaningful reweighting of violation-inducing tokens. If random or disabled variants perform similarly, or if the head attends mostly to irrelevant tokens, the proposed mechanism is not supported even if overall safety improves. This experiment could be made unnecessary if the claimant released the trained head, architecture details, ablation results, and token-level attribution analyses showing that the head specifically identifies and reweights policy-risk tokens.

normalized.target_subclaim: Primarily subclaim 1 (the comparison baseline), with a secondary test of whether the safety change is accompanied by retained general helpfulness.
normalized.method: Run the same base LLM unmodified and with the proposed attention-head intervention on a public safety dataset, using identical prompts, decoding, and evaluation criteria; score with an automated safety classifier plus a human-audited subset, and optionally assess utility on MT-Bench or AlpacaEval.
normalized.measurement: Policy-violation rate for base versus augmented model; general utility/helpfulness on MT-Bench or AlpacaEval.
normalized.decision_rule: No exact 50% decision rule is stated. A 'substantially lower' violation rate would support the comparison claim, while disappearance under matched controls would weaken it.

reasoning_chain: [1] The claim requires a paired comparison to an unmodified version of the same LLM, with the claimed attention-head change isolated from prompt, decoding, and other model changes.

[2] Experiment 0 does specify identical prompts, decoding settings, and evaluation criteria, and says not to change system prompts, refusal templates, RLHF weights, or decoding parameters; this makes its comparison directionally useful.

[3] It does not identify the checkpoint, tokenizer/chat template, exact head architecture, insertion point, training procedure, or parameter-freezing/integrity checks, so the experiment does not yet establish that the augmented condition differs only by the claimed one-head intervention.
[4] ASR/PVR is an appropriate behavior-level endpoint: HarmBench defines ASR as the percentage of test cases eliciting the target behavior (E0).

[5] The proposed alternatives are not equally suitable: AdvBench is a public harmful-behavior resource with an attempt-based success criterion (E3), but hh-rlhf is human preference data about helpfulness and harmlessness rather than a standardized held-out policy-violation benchmark (E4).

[6] The experiment never pre-specifies the claimed 50% relative-reduction threshold, a fixed evaluation corpus, a model scope, or an exact label criterion, so a lower rate would provide useful evidence but would not decide the numerical claim.
[7] MT-Bench is a real multi-turn quality benchmark (E5), so it can be a useful anti-over-refusal/utility control, but utility preservation does not substitute for a safety decision rule.
[8] Therefore the experiment would produce useful baseline-comparison information, but its underspecified apparatus and absent quantitative rule make it MIXED rather than ACCURATE.

normalized.target_subclaim: Subclaim 2: whether the policy-violation rate falls by at least 50% relative to the unmodified LLM.
normalized.method: Evaluate base and augmented models on held-out HarmBench, AdvBench, and JailbreakBench prompts; compute (PVR_base-PVR_head)/PVR_base; use bootstrap confidence intervals and McNemar's test on paired outcomes.
normalized.measurement: Paired prompt-level policy-violation rates and relative reduction; bootstrap interval and McNemar test.
normalized.decision_rule: A lower confidence bound above 50% on at least one broad benchmark supports the quantitative claim; a point estimate below 50% or an interval compatible with much smaller reductions does not establish it. The rule is not fully specified for all possible interval outcomes or model/dataset cells.

reasoning_chain: [1] The proposed relative-reduction formula is the correct interpretation of 'reduced by 50%' as a relative rather than percentage-point reduction.
[2] HarmBench supplies an appropriate behavior-level ASR/PVR endpoint (E0), and AdvBench is a public harmful-behavior benchmark with an explicit attempt-based success criterion (E3).
[3] Paired prompt outcomes, confidence intervals, and McNemar's test are useful for quantifying a paired base-versus-head change rather than merely comparing unrelated aggregate rates.

[4] The experiment says to use held-out prompts, which is directionally correct, but it does not specify the exact model checkpoint, chat template, decoding rule, generation length, or the exact trained head; those choices can change the measured rate.

[5] Generation length is not a harmless omitted detail: HarmBench reports that the parameter can change ASR by up to 30% and standardizes it to N=512 (E1). Thus 'held-out public datasets' alone does not make the result reproducible or fairly paired.

[6] JailbreakBench specifically states that proper evaluation of a test-time defense should use attacks tailored to the defense, and that transfer attacks from undefended models only give a lower bound on worst-case ASR (E2). A static jailbreak-oriented dataset therefore does not test adaptive robustness of this token-reweighting defense.

[7] The rule 'at least one broad benchmark' could support a narrowly pre-registered existential result, but it does not meet the stronger reference scope requiring fixed model families and both direct and defense-aware adaptive conditions; the experiment does not say which model or model family is being tested.
[8] Consequently it would yield useful quantitative evidence and is substantially on the right track, but it cannot by itself verify or refute the claim as operationalized, so the verdict is MIXED.

normalized.target_subclaim: Subclaims 3 and 4: whether the intervention is an additional attention head and whether it selectively reweights tokens likely to induce policy violations.
normalized.method: Implement an inspectable head/token-scoring mechanism; train or calibrate it with harmful and benign data; compare unmodified, active-head, random/shuffled-head, and reweighting-disabled variants on held-out safety prompts; inspect high-scoring tokens using human or classifier rationales; and mask/suppress those tokens as a causal check.
normalized.measurement: Safety outcomes for ablations, concentration of scores on policy-relevant tokens, and effects of suppressing/masking high-scoring tokens.
normalized.decision_rule: The active learned head should uniquely reduce violations and concentrate scores on policy-relevant tokens; similar performance from random or disabled variants, or attention to irrelevant tokens, would count against the mechanism. No numerical thresholds or statistical test are specified.

reasoning_chain: [1] The mechanism claim is stronger than observing a safer output: it requires that an added attention head reweight tokens likely to induce violations, rather than merely adding parameters or causing generic refusal.

[2] Inspectable scores, active/disabled comparisons, shuffled controls, token-level annotation, and masking/deletion can provide useful information about selectivity and causal relevance; this is therefore not an irrelevant experiment.

[3] However, the proposal does not specify that the intervention is literally one new causal attention head with all original weights frozen, nor does it specify the head equation, insertion location, output path, or an integrity test that the disabled version exactly reproduces the base model.

[4] The proposed 'randomly initialized or shuffled' condition combines two different controls: a randomly initialized head may alter the residual computation simply because it is a live random module, while shuffling learned scores is a more direct token-selection control. Without separating and matching these interventions, success cannot be attributed uniquely to selective token reweighting.

[5] Training/calibrating with HarmBench and then evaluating on 'held-out public safety prompts' is not enough to establish held-outness: no split, source-group separation, semantic deduplication, or locked evaluation judge is specified, leaving leakage and evaluator tuning possible.

[6] OpenAssistant and Alpaca are real public instruction/dialogue resources, but neither is by itself a validated benign policy benchmark; OpenAssistant is general multilingual dialogue data (E6), and Alpaca is instruction data generated by text-davinci-003 (E7). They can supply generic benign training examples, but they do not establish that the benign contrast is policy-aligned or that the head avoids over-refusal.

[7] The experiment has no pre-specified 50% PVR threshold and no adaptive attack evaluation, so even a positive mechanism result would not verify the headline numerical claim or robustness to a defense-aware attacker.
[8] Thus it can produce meaningful mechanistic evidence, but it is under-specified and cannot alone establish either the exact apparatus or the overall claim; MIXED is the appropriate verdict.

reasoning_chain: [1] The claim includes a mechanistic assertion about an added attention head reweighting violation-inducing tokens, so an inspectable active-versus-disabled/shuffled ablation and token-level analysis would produce useful information about subclaims 3 and 4.

[2] There is field precedent for attention-based token reweighting: DETAM reports amplifying core-intention-token positions with a scaling factor while leaving other positions unchanged (E7). This makes the proposed mechanistic direction plausible rather than facially irrelevant.

[3] The proposal does not require that all original model parameters remain frozen, does not define exactly one additional causal head, and does not specify a zero-gate/base-logit integrity check; therefore an improvement could still be caused by an unspecified extra module or inadvertent fine-tuning.

[4] 'Randomly initialized or shuffled' is ambiguous and is not a matched parameter/control condition, while masking or deleting high-scoring tokens can change the meaning of the harmful prompt rather than isolate the head's causal action.
[5] The proposal also omits the claim's quantitative 50% relative threshold and gives no exact held-out split or adaptive-attack condition, so it cannot by itself establish the full numerical claim.

[6] OpenAssistant is a general human-feedback conversation resource (E4), not a validated benign-refusal control; using it as generic benign instruction data is possible, but it cannot substitute for a specified benign safety test.

[7] These omissions weaken attribution and completeness but the active/disabled/shuffled comparison and token analysis still yield useful mechanistic evidence, so the verdict is MIXED rather than IRRELEVANT.

normalized.method: Run the same base LLM unmodified and with the proposed attention-head intervention on a public safety dataset, using identical prompts, decoding, and evaluation criteria; score with an automated safety classifier plus a human-audited subset, and optionally assess utility on MT-Bench or AlpacaEval.

reasoning_chain: [1] The claim requires a paired comparison to an unmodified version of the same LLM, with the claimed attention-head change isolated from prompt, decoding, and other model changes.

[2] Experiment 0 does specify identical prompts, decoding settings, and evaluation criteria, and says not to change system prompts, refusal templates, RLHF weights, or decoding parameters; this makes its comparison directionally useful.

[3] It does not identify the checkpoint, tokenizer/chat template, exact head architecture, insertion point, training procedure, or parameter-freezing/integrity checks, so the experiment does not yet establish that the augmented condition differs only by the claimed one-head intervention.
[4] ASR/PVR is an appropriate behavior-level endpoint: HarmBench defines ASR as the percentage of test cases eliciting the target behavior (E0).

[5] The proposed alternatives are not equally suitable: AdvBench is a public harmful-behavior resource with an attempt-based success criterion (E3), but hh-rlhf is human preference data about helpfulness and harmlessness rather than a standardized held-out policy-violation benchmark (E4).

[6] The experiment never pre-specifies the claimed 50% relative-reduction threshold, a fixed evaluation corpus, a model scope, or an exact label criterion, so a lower rate would provide useful evidence but would not decide the numerical claim.
[7] MT-Bench is a real multi-turn quality benchmark (E5), so it can be a useful anti-over-refusal/utility control, but utility preservation does not substitute for a safety decision rule.
[8] Therefore the experiment would produce useful baseline-comparison information, but its underspecified apparatus and absent quantitative rule make it MIXED rather than ACCURATE.

normalized.target_subclaim: Subclaim 2: whether the policy-violation rate falls by at least 50% relative to the unmodified LLM.
normalized.method: Evaluate base and augmented models on held-out HarmBench, AdvBench, and JailbreakBench prompts; compute (PVR_base-PVR_head)/PVR_base; use bootstrap confidence intervals and McNemar's test on paired outcomes.
normalized.measurement: Paired prompt-level policy-violation rates and relative reduction; bootstrap interval and McNemar test.
normalized.decision_rule: A lower confidence bound above 50% on at least one broad benchmark supports the quantitative claim; a point estimate below 50% or an interval compatible with much smaller reductions does not establish it. The rule is not fully specified for all possible interval outcomes or model/dataset cells.

reasoning_chain: [1] The proposed relative-reduction formula is the correct interpretation of 'reduced by 50%' as a relative rather than percentage-point reduction.
[2] HarmBench supplies an appropriate behavior-level ASR/PVR endpoint (E0), and AdvBench is a public harmful-behavior benchmark with an explicit attempt-based success criterion (E3).
[3] Paired prompt outcomes, confidence intervals, and McNemar's test are useful for quantifying a paired base-versus-head change rather than merely comparing unrelated aggregate rates.

[4] The experiment says to use held-out prompts, which is directionally correct, but it does not specify the exact model checkpoint, chat template, decoding rule, generation length, or the exact trained head; those choices can change the measured rate.

[5] Generation length is not a harmless omitted detail: HarmBench reports that the parameter can change ASR by up to 30% and standardizes it to N=512 (E1). Thus 'held-out public datasets' alone does not make the result reproducible or fairly paired.

[6] JailbreakBench specifically states that proper evaluation of a test-time defense should use attacks tailored to the defense, and that transfer attacks from undefended models only give a lower bound on worst-case ASR (E2). A static jailbreak-oriented dataset therefore does not test adaptive robustness of this token-reweighting defense.

[7] The rule 'at least one broad benchmark' could support a narrowly pre-registered existential result, but it does not meet the stronger reference scope requiring fixed model families and both direct and defense-aware adaptive conditions; the experiment does not say which model or model family is being tested.
[8] Consequently it would yield useful quantitative evidence and is substantially on the right track, but it cannot by itself verify or refute the claim as operationalized, so the verdict is MIXED.

normalized.target_subclaim: Subclaims 3 and 4: whether the intervention is an additional attention head and whether it selectively reweights tokens likely to induce policy violations.
normalized.method: Implement an inspectable head/token-scoring mechanism; train or calibrate it with harmful and benign data; compare unmodified, active-head, random/shuffled-head, and reweighting-disabled variants on held-out safety prompts; inspect high-scoring tokens using human or classifier rationales; and mask/suppress those tokens as a causal check.
normalized.measurement: Safety outcomes for ablations, concentration of scores on policy-relevant tokens, and effects of suppressing/masking high-scoring tokens.
normalized.decision_rule: The active learned head should uniquely reduce violations and concentrate scores on policy-relevant tokens; similar performance from random or disabled variants, or attention to irrelevant tokens, would count against the mechanism. No numerical thresholds or statistical test are specified.

reasoning_chain: [1] The mechanism claim is stronger than observing a safer output: it requires that an added attention head reweight tokens likely to induce violations, rather than merely adding parameters or causing generic refusal.

[2] Inspectable scores, active/disabled comparisons, shuffled controls, token-level annotation, and masking/deletion can provide useful information about selectivity and causal relevance; this is therefore not an irrelevant experiment.

[3] However, the proposal does not specify that the intervention is literally one new causal attention head with all original weights frozen, nor does it specify the head equation, insertion location, output path, or an integrity test that the disabled version exactly reproduces the base model.

[4] The proposed 'randomly initialized or shuffled' condition combines two different controls: a randomly initialized head may alter the residual computation simply because it is a live random module, while shuffling learned scores is a more direct token-selection control. Without separating and matching these interventions, success cannot be attributed uniquely to selective token reweighting.

[5] Training/calibrating with HarmBench and then evaluating on 'held-out public safety prompts' is not enough to establish held-outness: no split, source-group separation, semantic deduplication, or locked evaluation judge is specified, leaving leakage and evaluator tuning possible.

[6] OpenAssistant and Alpaca are real public instruction/dialogue resources, but neither is by itself a validated benign policy benchmark; OpenAssistant is general multilingual dialogue data (E6), and Alpaca is instruction data generated by text-davinci-003 (E7). They can supply generic benign training examples, but they do not establish that the benign contrast is policy-aligned or that the head avoids over-refusal.

[7] The experiment has no pre-specified 50% PVR threshold and no adaptive attack evaluation, so even a positive mechanism result would not verify the headline numerical claim or robustness to a defense-aware attacker.
[8] Thus it can produce meaningful mechanistic evidence, but it is under-specified and cannot alone establish either the exact apparatus or the overall claim; MIXED is the appropriate verdict.

[5] Direct held-out prompts do not test an attacker optimized against the augmented model, so this does not establish adaptive robustness under the stronger reference scope.
[6] It remains useful direct quantitative evidence, but is under-specified and insufficient alone: MIXED.

normalized.method: Use inspectable head scores; compare unmodified, active learned, random/shuffled, and reweighting-disabled variants; compare high-score tokens with human/classifier rationales and mask or suppress high-score tokens on held-out safety prompts.
normalized.measurement: Safety outcomes across ablations, token-rationale agreement, and behavioral effect of masking high-scoring tokens.
normalized.decision_rule: The active learned head and policy-relevant token concentration support the mechanism; similar random/disabled performance or irrelevant attention argues against it. Exact thresholds and architecture are absent.

reasoning_chain: [1] Inspectable scores and learned-versus-disabled/shuffled comparisons are directionally appropriate tests of the proposed mechanism.
[2] HarmBench is an appropriate harmful-behavior source, and OpenAssistant and Stanford Alpaca resources exist for general instruction or benign data (E8 and E10).

[3] The design does not require exactly one new causal head, frozen original weights, or a precise insertion and training specification, so a positive result could reflect an unspecified architectural change or fine-tuning.
[4] Random/shuffled and disabled variants are not precisely defined or matched, so their outcomes would not cleanly separate token reweighting from extra parameters or residual-path effects.
[5] Masking high-score tokens can destroy the harmful request's semantics, so a reduction after masking is not by itself causal evidence for the attention mechanism.

[6] No held-out mechanism split, exact risk-token definition, generation-time attention enrichment measure, or anti-over-refusal control is specified; the experiment is useful mechanistic evidence but not decisive attribution: MIXED.

runs.sufficiency_reasoning: The set would produce useful direct safety, utility, and mechanistic evidence. It would not decide the claim as written because the exact base checkpoint and literal one-head architecture are not fixed, safety judges and held-out splits are not locked, the 50% rule is absent or discretionary in Experiments 0 and 2 and only partly fixed in Experiment 1, and the masking test can confound semantic destruction with causal token reweighting. Under the reference's stronger scope, it also lacks defense-aware adaptive attacks.
